claim: DfE's Generative AI product safety standards, updated 19 January 2026, contain 13 standards, including cognitive development (no final answers, full solutions or complete worked examples by default; track offloading), emotional and social development (function-based language, no human persona) and manipulation (no unjustified confidence).
source: Department for Education (2026). Generative AI: product safety standards. GOV.UK, updated 19 January 2026.
population: England, products used by learners
recommendation: Pitch: eduX already tracks a self-chosen offloading proxy (the just-show-me choice) and teaches hint-first for course questions. It does not detect pasted or copied answers; say so if asked. - State why factual research questions get a full answer plus a checking task (05e). Don't lean on the withdrawn Khanmigo claim. - Check that `text/` describes the chatbot in function-based terms.

Emotional and social development: function-based phrasing, no names or avatars implying personhood. Manipulation: avoid 'absolute, or unjustified confidence'.

population: adults, workplace; not 16–18, not UK

mark_note: arXiv abstract and HTML full text (Table 4): single author Daniele Veri'; 24 focal empirical publications; three direct subjective-objective correlations, REML r = .055, Hartung-Knapp 95% CI [-.047, .156], combined N = 2,765; workplace adults. Unrefereed preprint, and all three correlations come from one research programme.

claim: In Newton's Playground, gold-trophy counts per agent correlated r = .22–.40 with a physics pretest (silver .03–.29), the physics test had Cronbach's alpha .72/.73, and pre-post gain was t(154) = 2.12, p < .05.
source: Shute, V. J., Ventura, M., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Assessment and learning of qualitative physics in Newton's Playground. Journal of Educational Research, 106(6), 423-430.
effect: gold-trophy r with pretest: ramp .27, lever .22, pendulum .31, springboard .40 (N = 166); pre–post gain t(154) = 2.12, p < .05; pretest–posttest r = .60
population: 167 US 8th–9th graders (about 13–15), one university lab school, about 4 h of play over 1.5 weeks. Not UK, younger than 16–18
recommendation: Use as the benchmark: single in-game indicators correlate about .2–.4 with an external test. Present eduX's target in the same range.
risk: credibility, if we imply our scores are already validated. They're not.
mark_note: Full text: 167 grade 8-9 students at Florida State University School, about 4 h; Table 3 (N = 166) gold .27/.22/.31/.40 and silver .16/.03/.06/.29; Forms A and B are 12 items each, alpha .72/.73; t(154) = 2.12, p < .05; pre-post r = .60. All match.

claim: A stealth assessment of problem solving in Use Your Brainz correlated r = .40 with Raven's Progressive Matrices and r = .41 with MicroDYN (n = 47), with Cronbach's alpha .76 across its four facets.
source: Shute, V. J., Wang, L., Greiff, S., Zhao, W., & Moore, G. (2016). Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game. Computers in Human Behavior, 63, 106-117.
population: 55 US 7th graders (47 analysed), one suburban Illinois school, about 3 h of play. Not UK, younger
recommendation: Cite as the model study design: hours of naturalistic evidence, then two external tests. Our pilot copies this shape.
risk: small n, so wide CI (about .13–.62)
mark_note: Full text: 55 7th graders at a middle school in suburban Illinois, about 3 h on iPad; with n = 47, r = 0.40 (Raven's) and r = 0.41 (MicroDYN), both p < .01; alpha 0.76 across the four facets. All match.

Verifier: 890 results confirmed, but they are configurations x 10 ASAP-SAS items, not results pooled across studies. The 0.37 decoder-encoder gap is on the Fisher-z scale, not raw QWK; the paper says so, and the frequentist estimate is -0.14 and not significant. claim: With single-item reliability of about .17 (back-solved from GLAT alpha .80 with 20 items and a physics test alpha .72 with 12 items), Spearman-Brown implies about 12 observed moments for reliability .70 and 20 for .80, rising to 18 and 30 if per-moment reliability is .12.
source: First-principles calculation: Spearman (1910) and Brown (1910), British Journal of Psychology 3; inputs from Jin et al. (2024) and Shute, Ventura & Kim (2013).
population: n/a
recommendation: Report `n_moments` and "provisional" in progress until about 8 moments (our choice). In the pitch, say how long that takes at a realistic research-question rate.
before_thursday: pitch yes; build once 05e is merged (it is built on branch build/05e-literacy-coaching, not merged to main)
risk: assumes parallel, independent moments. Ask moments come from the same student's similar questions, so reliability may be higher (consistency) or the score narrower (construct under-representation)
mark_note: before_thursday reworded per coordinator: 05e is built on its branch, not merged. Verifier: Recomputed. Back-solved rho1 = .80/(20-19*.80) = .167; .72 with 12 items (NP Form A, confirmed 12 items) gives .176. Spearman-Brown k = R(1-r)/(r(1-R)): at .17, 11.4 -> 12 and 19.5 -> 20; at .12, 17.1 -> 18 and 29.3 -> 30.

claim: eduX's AI-literacy parts use the course decay (base half-life 2 days, doubled on success), so a part at 0.75 after one correct moment falls to about 0.22 a week later.

claim: On a four-option opportunity-cost item, only 21.6% of 199 economists and PhD students at the 2005 ASSA meetings chose the intended answer ($10), while the wrong options $0, $40 and $50 drew 25.1%, 25.6% and 27.6%.
source: Ferraro, P.J. & Taylor, L.O. (2005). Do economists recognize an opportunity cost when they see one? A dismal performance from the dismal science. Contributions to Economic Analysis & Policy 4(1), Article 7.

recommendation: Use the structure (one key and three single-error distractors) as the demo opportunity-cost check, written in our own UK wording. Add rows 1–3.

claim: Among 358 US students in the first week of introductory microeconomics, those who had taken a previous economics course answered the opportunity-cost item correctly less often (7.4%) than those who had not (17.2%), a significant difference (chi-squared 7.13, p = 0.008).

mark_note: Full text: 358 undergraduates in week 1 of Intro Micro; 270 (76%) with a prior macro or high-school course, 86 (24%) without; 7.4% vs 17.2% correct; Pearson chi2 = 7.13, p = 0.008.

claim: In 431 first-year students, the opportunity-cost subscore on the Test of Economic Literacy barely changed over a semester (mean 3.58 to 3.68 out of 5), acquisition depended more on background than on teaching, and it was only weakly related to final course performance.
source: Shanahan, M.P., Foster, G. & Meyer, J.H.F. (2006). Operationalising a threshold concept in economics: a pilot study using multiple choice questions on opportunity cost. International Review of Economics Education 5(2), 29-57.

risk: credibility (pilot measure with acknowledged measurement error)
mark_note: Full text: UniSA introductory economics, n = 431; first TEL OC 3.58 (1.29), last 3.68 (1.23), difference 0.10 (1.42), scale 0-5. The conclusion states acquisition depends more on background than the classroom and is weakly related to final performance. r = .45 is OC exam level vs final percent; the OC change vs final percent is r = .01.

claim: Davies and Mangan classify marginality, opportunity cost, incentives and cumulative causation as discipline threshold concepts in economics, and comparative statics (equilibrium, ceteris paribus), time and elasticity as modelling concepts, and recommend assessing them with unfamiliar problems that do not name the model.

claim: In the TUCE-4 matched norming sample, 43% before and 32% after a principles course chose business demand as the limit of productive capacity, 36% before and 28% after chose falling long-run economic profits when competitive firms' costs rise, and 33% before and 29% after chose that firms would pay a pollution tax rather than cut production; overall percent correct rose from about 31-33% to 43-47%.

claim: At the start of term, 69% (control) and 77% (treatment) of first-year economics students agreed that rent controls make housing available to more families; information reduced but did not eliminate this belief. source: Brandts, J., Busom, I., Lopez-Mayan, C. & Panadés, J. (2022). Dispelling misconceptions about economics. Journal of Economic Psychology 88, 102461 (doi:10.1016/j.joep.2021.102461); figures from the BSE Focus summary 'Dispelling Misconceptions about Rent Control'.

recommendation: Add row 12. Because a single correction partly fades, keep the misconception in reviews: correct evidence clears it, but a review re-tests it.

Verifier: Checked against the authors' BSE Focus summary only: 69% control and 77% treatment at the start (UAB, 340/272); lab 84/75/83% (Valencia, n = 172); disagreement rose 16-22%; the belief was not eliminated. claim: In Mayer's summary table of multimedia-learning experiments, coherence had a median effect size of 0.86 (18 of 19 tests positive), signaling 0.70 (26 of 28), segmenting 0.67 (7 of 7), pre-training 0.78 (10 of 10), modality 1.00 (18 of 19) and redundancy 0.10 (8 of 12).
source: Mayer, R. E. Research-based principles for designing multimedia instruction. Chapter in Society for the Teaching of Psychology e-book Applying the Science of Learning in Education (updated edition; tables based on Mayer, 2021, Multimedia Learning, 3rd ed., Cambridge University Press)
evidence_strength: theory (a narrative summary of the author's own experiments, with median effect sizes; not a systematic meta-analysis)
effect: median d: coherence 0.86, signalling 0.70, segmenting 0.67, pre-training 0.78, modality 1.00, redundancy 0.10; no CIs reported
population: mostly university students in lab experiments, US. Not 16–18 and not UK.
recommendation: Build the video as seven labelled segments, with one keyword and one highlight box per shot, no music or stock footage, a pre-training diagram before the demo, and narration as the main channel (captions as a separate track). Applying this to persuading judges is our analogy.
risk: credibility, if presented as evidence that the *pitch* works. These are lab learning effects, and the author's own summary may be optimistic compared with independent meta-analyses (see 02 and 03).
mark_note: Full text Tables 2 and 3 (based on Mayer 2021): coherence 18 of 19, 0.86; signaling 26 of 28, 0.70; redundancy 8 of 12, 0.10; segmenting 7 of 7, 0.67; pre-training 10 of 10, 0.78; modality 18 of 19, 1.00. Population 'mostly US university students' is not stated in the chapter.

claim: A meta-analysis of 44 independent effect sizes from 29 experimental studies with 2,726 participants found signaling associated with increased learning outcomes, d = 0.38.

effect: d = 0.38 (p < .01); CI not in the abstract
population: mixed grade levels (coded as a moderator); not UK-specific
recommendation: Keep the highlight boxes on the plan's first line and on the `state` row that changes. Use one cue at a time.
risk: low. Over-signalling (many cues) is a known boundary condition.
mark_note: Abstract-level only (publisher page paywalled; abstract text seen via search snippets): 44 effect sizes, 29 studies, 2,726 participants, d = .38, p < .01. ETR&D 68(5):2095-2119. Not retracted (OpenAlex).

claim: A signaling meta-analysis (reported as 103 studies, 12,201 participants) found cues improved retention g = 0.53 and transfer g = 0.33 (figures from secondary reports).

population: mostly university students; not UK
recommendation: Signalling helps people remember *what* was shown more than reason with it. Use it for the one fact judges must retain ("server never calls an AI model"; "the letter is scored by the server").
risk: the numbers are unverified against the primary source; cite as secondary.
mark_note: Secondary source only (TUM Clearing House Unterricht summary): 103 studies, 12,201 participants (~14% secondary pupils), retention g = 0.53, transfer g = 0.33 (70 comparisons). CIs and k=139 not checked. Published 2018 (online 2017), ERR 23:1-24.

effect: "small to medium" (no numbers in the abstract)
population: mostly university students; not UK
recommendation: Seven named segments, with a keyword change at each cut (§A). In the live demo, pause after each reply and say what changed before the next message. Already cited in step 05d for teaching; here it is reused for the video.

claim: A meta-analysis found that including seductive details (interesting but irrelevant information) in learning materials can hinder learning, with effects moderated by factors including learner pacing and delivery format.

population: mixed; not UK-specific
recommendation: No stock footage of classrooms, no music under narration, and no team-backstory shots in the 2:30. Put the team on the end card only.
risk: low. Builds on 1-14; not new evidence.
mark_note: Secondary only (publisher abstract not readable). ACU Inspire summary: 68 effects from 58 studies, g = -0.33; larger negative effect when learners cannot control pace, and for static details, text+image, and paper vs digital. Consistent with claim. EPR 32(3):707-734.

claim: In eight hospitals in eight cities, introducing a 19-item surgical safety checklist was associated with deaths falling from 1.5% to 0.8% and inpatient complications from 11.0% to 7.0%, comparing 3,733 patients before with 3,955 after.

risk: low. Don't cite it in the pitch; it's a team-process tool.
mark_note: Abstract only (cap): 19-item checklist, 8 hospitals in 8 cities (8 countries), 3,733 before / 3,955 after, patients 16+, noncardiac surgery; deaths 1.5% -> 0.8% (P=0.003); complications 11.0% -> 7.0% (P<0.001). All numbers match. NEJM 360(5):491-499.

claim: Degani and Wiener's NASA contractor report analyses the functions, format, design, length and use of the normal flight-deck checklist against human limitations and ends with design guidelines.

Verifier: Tunguz page confirms pitches 'oscillate between what is and what could be' but does not mention ending with the reward ('new bliss'). claim: For a school-randomised trial with 20 students per school, ICC 0.15, R-squared 0.5 at both levels, 80% power and 5% two-sided significance (multiplier 2.8), the minimum detectable effect size is about 0.39 SD with 20 schools, 0.27 with 40, 0.22 with 60, 0.19 with 80 and 0.17 with 100.
source: Our calculation using the two-level MDES formula in Bloom, Richburg-Hayes & Black (2007), Using covariates to improve precision for studies that randomize schools to evaluate educational interventions, Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis 29(1)
population: hypothetical English Year 12–13 Economics classes
recommendation: Evaluation slide: a feasibility pilot (3–5 schools) now, then an efficacy trial of about 60–100 schools with an independent evaluator. Never claim a pilot shows learning gains.
risk: credibility, if the ICC or R² are presented as measured. Real A level ICCs should be checked against EEF guidance. M = 2.8 is the large-sample multiplier. With about 20 schools (about 17 school-level df), M is about 2.9–3.0, so the 20-school MDES is about 0.40–0.42; the conclusion doesn't change.
mark_note: Recomputed MDES = 2.8*sqrt(rho(1-R2)/(P(1-P)J) + (1-rho)(1-R2)/(P(1-P)Jn)), P=0.5: 0.388/0.275/0.224/0.194/0.174 at J=20/40/60/80/100. Matches. Caveat: M=2.8 is the large-df multiplier; with J=20 (df~18) M is ~2.98, giving ~0.41. Bloom et al. 2007 EEPA 29(1):30-59 exists.

England.
